overview:
Crown rule over India began as damage control. After the rebellion of 1857 nearly broke the East India Company's hold on northern India, Parliament passed the Government of India Act in August 1858, abolishing Company government and transferring its territories, armies and revenues to the Crown. A Secretary of State for India in London, advised by a council, now directed policy; in Calcutta the Governor-General was restyled Viceroy, Lord Canning first among them. Queen Victoria's proclamation that November promised non-interference in religion and permanent support for the surviving Indian princes — a settlement that left roughly two-fifths of the subcontinent's territory and about a third of its people under some 500-odd princely rulers bound by treaty to British paramountcy, while the rest was administered directly through provinces and a small, overwhelmingly British Indian Civil Service. At its greatest extent the Raj reached from Baluchistan to Burma, with Ceylon, Nepal and the small French and Portuguese enclaves outside it.

The economy the Raj built was oriented outward. Railways, canals, telegraphs and ports were laid down on a scale unmatched anywhere in Asia, but the traffic they carried — raw cotton, jute, wheat, opium, tea — moved toward British markets, while Lancashire cloth moved the other way and Indian handloom weaving contracted. Land revenue settlements pushed the risk of a bad monsoon onto cultivators. The result was recurring catastrophe: the famines of 1876–78 and 1899–1900 killed millions and provoked the Famine Codes of 1880, and the Bengal famine of 1943, with estimates running from under a million to around three million dead, is now widely judged by historians a failure of wartime policy and distribution rather than of harvests. Against this, an English-educated professional class turned the empire's own liberal vocabulary back on it. The Indian National Congress met first in 1885, the All-India Muslim League formed in 1906, the Swadeshi boycott followed Curzon's partition of Bengal, and after Gandhi's return in 1915 mass non-cooperation replaced petitioning. Repression — the Amritsar massacre of 1919, the jailing of the Congress leadership after Quit India in 1942 — hardened rather than dispersed the movement.

Two world wars drained the arrangement of both money and legitimacy. India supplied more than a million men to the first and over two million volunteers to the second, and by 1945 Britain owed India large sterling balances rather than the reverse. Constitutional concessions had come in slow instalments — Morley-Minto in 1909, Montagu-Chelmsford in 1919, the Government of India Act of 1935 — each conceding elected Indian participation while reserving real power, and each embedding separate electorates that sharpened the communal question. When Attlee's government resolved to leave, Mountbatten pulled the deadline forward to August 1947. Cyril Radcliffe drew boundaries through Punjab and Bengal in a matter of weeks; India and Pakistan became independent on 15 and 14 August. Somewhere between twelve and twenty million people were displaced and estimates of the dead range from around 200,000 to two million.
significance: The Raj is the template case for how modern empire actually worked — not by occupying every village but by ruling through law courts, revenue records, railways, a census that fixed fluid identities into countable categories, and local elites bound by treaty. Its end in 1947 was the largest single transfer of power in the history of decolonisation and set the terms for everything that followed: three nation-states where one administrative unit had stood, a Kashmir dispute inherited directly from the princely settlement, and a partition trauma still politically live. Its economic legacy remains the central battleground in arguments about whether colonialism developed or drained the societies it governed, and Indian nationalism's methods — mass non-violent non-cooperation above all — were studied and reused by anti-colonial and civil rights movements from Ghana to the American South.
coverage: Written from general reference accounts of Crown rule, partition and the 1943 Bengal famine; the dataset itself holds no events under this story, so the map can show none of the ninety years described here. The surviving record is enormous but lopsided: the India Office Records run to roughly nine miles of shelving, almost all of it generated by the colonial state, while famine mortality, partition death tolls and the internal history of the princely states rest on estimates that serious historians place within wide and contested ranges.
